scope: every workspace member listed in the root Cargo.toml, its Cargo.toml parsed by dependency section, and its non-test Rust source outside core — its src tree and its Cargo build script — excluding inline cfg(test) modules, files under a tests directory, and files named test*.rs

decision.summary: The orchestrator database has one persistence layer: core today, orchestrator-persistence after FR-130 Phase A. Crates above that layer may not reach the driver; the two that do today carry a frozen residual until FR-130 pays it down. The line is drawn at the database rather than at the crate graph because two of the six driver-holding crates are not above the layer at all: orchestrator-security sits below core, and slack-gateway owns a different database.
decision.decisiveCase: crates/orchestrator-scheduler/src/scheduler/task_state.rs holds eight production driver references inside scheduling logic. It is forbidden. FR-136 states that if even this file may stay where it is, the form chosen is really B; it may not.

rejectedForms.A: Strict: only orchestrator-persistence names the driver. Rejected because core depends on orchestrator-security, so strict A requires persistence to sit below security or the edge to be inverted, and because slack-gateway has no workspace dependencies and its own database — strict A would manufacture an edge for a database that shares nothing with this one.
rejectedForms.B: Controlled sharing: freeze today's list, review additions. Rejected because it leaves task_state.rs in place, which FR-136 names as the test for whether a decision is really B.

core.reason: was the persistence layer until FR-130 Phase A moved the code into crates/orchestrator-persistence, which inherited the role; this entry went on saying core *is* the layer for four FRs after it stopped being true. FR-141 finished the move: no production file in core names the driver, and the declaration is under [dev-dependencies], where its users are cfg(test) modules asserting on rows core logic wrote through orchestrator-persistence test_support

crates/cli.reason: no relationship to persistence; reaching for the driver here would be a new consumer, not a residual

crates/daemon.reason: sits above core and used to borrow its AsyncDatabase connection to run raw SQL in gRPC handlers. FR-141 B2 moved every statement into the layer and B5 moved the cfg(test) modules that were still reading the database onto orchestrator-persistence test_support, so this crate no longer names the driver in any section of its manifest. `none` rather than `forbidden`: forbidden permits a [dev-dependencies] declaration, and there is nothing left here to declare it for

crates/gui.reason: no relationship to persistence; reaching for the driver here would be a new consumer, not a residual

crates/integration-tests.reason: declares the driver under [dev-dependencies] and uses it in tests/trigger_fire.rs to assert against the database directly, which is legitimate for a test. Frozen to the dev section so it cannot become a production dependency

crates/orchestrator-client.reason: no relationship to persistence; reaching for the driver here would be a new consumer, not a residual

crates/orchestrator-collab.reason: no relationship to persistence; reaching for the driver here would be a new consumer, not a residual

crates/orchestrator-config.reason: no relationship to persistence; reaching for the driver here would be a new consumer, not a residual

crates/orchestrator-persistence.reason: the persistence layer itself, as FR-130 Phase A. It owns agent_orchestrator.db: the connections that open it, the migration chain that shapes it, and the repositories that read and write it. Naming the driver here is the decision recorded above, not a residual to pay down

crates/orchestrator-runner.reason: no relationship to persistence; reaching for the driver here would be a new consumer, not a residual

crates/orchestrator-scheduler.reason: sits above core and used to borrow its AsyncDatabase connection to run raw SQL in scheduling logic, task_state.rs included — the file DD-147 named as the decisive case. FR-141 paid that residual to zero: no production file here names the driver, and the declaration moved to [dev-dependencies], where its remaining users are cfg(test) modules exercising statements that now live in the persistence layer. It goes entirely when FR-141 B5 relocates those tests, at which point this becomes `none`

crates/orchestrator-security.reason: core depends on orchestrator-security, not the reverse, so it cannot route through a layer above it. It opens the orchestrator database by path with its own synchronous connection and owns secret_keys, secret_key_audit and the encrypted resources rows. Frozen rather than migrated: inverting the edge to save six references is not proportionate

crates/proto.reason: no relationship to persistence; reaching for the driver here would be a new consumer, not a residual

crates/slack-gateway.reason: no workspace dependencies at all, and GatewayStore::open opens SLACK_GATEWAY_DATABASE, documented in config.rs as the gateway-owned database. Its 55 SQL statements never touch agent_orchestrator.db, so it is outside this chokepoint. Frozen so it cannot quietly begin opening the orchestrator database
